lessons.title: Your Roadmap
lessons.output: A small learning plan you can start today.
lessons.bring: No car, business paperwork or experience needed.
paragraphs: Your goal is not to finish a playlist. It is to build a rental process you can explain and practice.

Use the course in three moves: read one short lesson, try its worksheet, then check your answer. Start with one lesson per sitting. Short notes are enough. When you do not know something, write: “Unknown — [person] will [action] by [date].” That lets you keep learning while the real-world question stays open.

Fictional example: Maya has one car and no rental experience. Her goal is to rehearse a pickup, not launch tomorrow. She writes “Coverage unknown — I will arrange an insurance conversation this week.” She uses this browser for practice and downloads an answer backup after a module. A reviewed worksheet records learning; it does not approve her car for rental.
Your task: Write one goal, one open question and your next study session. Stop there; you do not need a complete business plan today.

questions.label: What do you want to be able to do?
questions.hint: Choose one action you could demonstrate to another person.
questions.example: Explain and rehearse a pickup from reservation checks to handing over keys.

questions.label: What are you starting with?
questions.hint: Name your vehicle, process or experience. “Starting from zero” is a valid answer.
questions.example: One car; no rental process yet.

questions.label: What is your first unanswered question?
questions.hint: Name the question and one next action; you do not have to solve it today.
questions.example: Is my intended rental use covered? I will contact an insurance professional this week.

questions.label: Where will you keep your answers and backup?
questions.hint: Answers stay in this browser. Lessons & tools → Download answers saves a separate file.
questions.example: Practice on this phone; download a backup to my private course folder after each module.

questions.label: When is your next learning session?
questions.hint: Choose a realistic day and one lesson, not a deadline for the entire course.
questions.example: Tomorrow after dinner: Lesson 0.2, then stop.

lessons.done: Write one goal, one open question and your next study session. Stop there; you do not need a complete business plan today.
lessons.time: Plan 10–15 minutes for a first draft; outside research can take longer.

lessons.title: Choose Your Starting Point
lessons.output: Your starting route and a list of operating locations.
lessons.bring: Your current situation; proposed locations are fine.
paragraphs: You do not need to start over if you already run rentals. You do need to know which parts of your process are verified.

If you are new, follow the lessons in order. If you already operate, use the roadmap to open a weak area and compare your current process with its worksheet. A familiar topic is only a reason to move faster, not to assume its checks are complete. List your main city, county and state, then any separate delivery or airport activity.

Fictional example: Maya starts from zero. She proposes local pickup in her home city; airport delivery is only an idea. She records the airport separately as “not offered; permission and coverage unverified.” An experienced owner with missing return photos could begin at 5.6, then revisit 3.5 for the related policy. Selecting a state does not verify any rule.
Your task: Choose a starting route, record your locations and pick one area to work on. If you have no existing process, write what you need to build first.

questions.label: Which starting route fits you?
questions.hint: Choose new owner or existing owner, then give one reason.
questions.example: New owner: I have not completed a rental before.

questions.label: Where will the business operate?
questions.hint: List city, county and state. Use a proposed location if you are still deciding.
questions.example: My city / my county / my state — proposed local pickup area.

questions.label: Where else might you offer pickup or delivery?
questions.hint: Separate planned service from ideas you have not checked.
questions.example: Local delivery is under investigation; not offered yet.

questions.label: Will you use an airport or cross state lines?
questions.hint: Write planned, not planned or unknown for each.
questions.example: Airport delivery: unknown. Interstate rental use: not planned for my first test.

questions.label: What process will you work on first?
questions.hint: New owners can start at 1.1; existing owners can name a gap and its lesson.
questions.example: Start at 1.1 to choose a customer situation before shopping for a car.

lessons.done: Choose a starting route, record your locations and pick one area to work on. If you have no existing process, write what you need to build first.
lessons.local: Record every operating city, county, state and special pickup area. Research permissions for each; the state picker is only a saved location preference.
lessons.time: Plan 10–15 minutes for a first draft; outside research can take longer.
lessons.revisionNote: Clarified the task, supplied a worked example and question-by-question guidance; preserved question meanings and saved-answer keys.

lessons.title: Choose Your Target Customer
lessons.output: One customer, one need, one proposed offer and one research action.
lessons.bring: A customer situation you can investigate.
paragraphs: Before you choose a car, choose who you want to help. Start with a customer situation you can investigate.

A customer profile is a testable idea about who needs a car and why. Use this sentence: “I want to help [person in a situation] who needs [specific help].” Describe the situation, such as waiting for a repair, rather than trying to serve everyone. Then name what you can realistically offer and one way to find out whether it matters.

Fictional example: Maya wants to serve local drivers whose cars are being repaired. She thinks predictable pickup and clear total pricing matter most. Her proposed offer is a temporary local rental with an explained handoff. She will compare nearby offers and ask two repair shops what customers struggle with. She has a hypothesis, not evidence of demand yet.
Your task: Write four short answers that fit together: customer → need → offer → research. You are done when your research could confirm or challenge your idea.

questions.label: Who do you want to serve?
questions.hint: Describe one customer situation. Avoid “everyone who needs a cheap car.”
questions.example: A local driver waiting several days for a car repair.

questions.label: What do they need most?
questions.hint: Pick one practical need you can investigate.
questions.example: Predictable pickup and an understandable total price.

questions.label: How could your rental help?
questions.hint: Describe a proposed service; do not promise unverified availability or coverage.
questions.example: A temporary local car with a clear pickup process and itemized quote.

questions.label: What will you research first?
questions.hint: Name an action, who or what you will consult, and when.
questions.example: This week, compare three nearby offers and ask two repair shops about transport questions.

lessons.done: Write four short answers that fit together: customer → need → offer → research. You are done when your research could confirm or challenge your idea.
lessons.time: Plan 10–15 minutes for a first draft; outside research can take longer.

lessons.title: Research Your Local Market
lessons.output: Three comparable offer notes and one finding.
lessons.bring: Your customer idea from 1.1; use the fictional practice offers if you cannot research today.
paragraphs: A low advertised daily price is not the whole rental offer. Compare like with like before drawing a conclusion.

Use the same vehicle category, dates, pickup/return times and pickup method for all three offers. Record the source and date, daily rate, displayed rental total, mileage terms and unanswered questions. Keep a refundable deposit separate. If a real total is unavailable, record “unknown”; do not place a booking just to finish the worksheet.

Practice dataset — all invented: three days, same local pickup, compact car. A: $40/day, $120 base, total unknown, mileage unknown. B: $50/day, $150 base, $165 displayed rental total, 300 miles included. C: $45/day, $135 base, total unknown, 200 miles included. Sources: practice cards A/B/C, reviewed today. B is the only complete displayed rental total; these notes cannot establish the cheapest real offer or prove demand.
Your task: Compare three real offers or label all three as fictional practice. Your finding must distinguish an observed number from a missing number. Save a research action for anything unknown.

questions.label: What customer and vehicle category are you comparing?
questions.hint: Reuse 1.1, then choose the same category for all three offers.
questions.example: Repair customer; compact car. Using fictional practice cards for this exercise.

questions.label: What matching dates and pickup conditions will you use?
questions.hint: Include times and rental length; a daily headline alone is not comparable.
questions.example: Day 1 at 09:00 to Day 4 at 09:00; three days; local pickup for all offers.

questions.label: Record offer A.
questions.hint: Use: source/date; daily price; base; displayed total; mileage; unknowns.
questions.example: Practice card A, today: $40/day; $120 base; total unknown; mileage unknown.

questions.label: Record offers B and C.
questions.hint: Put each on its own line using the same fields as A.
questions.example: Practice B, today: $50/day; $150 base; $165 displayed total; 300 miles. Practice C: $45/day; $135 base; total unknown; 200 miles.

questions.label: What did you learn, and what needs checking?
questions.hint: Do not rank complete prices when two totals are missing.
questions.example: Daily headlines differ, but only B has a displayed total. Research A/C totals before comparing complete costs.

lessons.done: Compare three real offers or label all three as fictional practice. Your finding must distinguish an observed number from a missing number. Save a research action for anything unknown.
lessons.time: Plan 10–15 minutes for a first draft; outside research can take longer.

lessons.title: Choose Your Operating Model
lessons.output: A responsibility map for your proposed operating model.
lessons.bring: One model to explore: owned car, leased car or another owner’s car.
paragraphs: Owning the car and operating the rental business are different responsibilities. Decide who does what before choosing your model.

Write one row per job: provide the car, manage bookings, handle customer questions, arrange maintenance and pay expenses during downtime. Name a responsible person or role for each. Downtime means time the car cannot earn from rentals. Ownership and day-to-day operation can belong to different people; the written arrangement must explain their responsibilities.

Fictional example: Jo supplies a car; Maya handles bookings and customer messages. They propose that Jo schedules service, but they have not agreed who pays for a repair or lost rental days. Their worksheet says “unresolved — both owners to review terms,” not “50/50 solves it.” Rental-use permission, coverage and the proposed written agreement need confirmation before use.
Your task: Choose one model and assign the main jobs. An honest unresolved row is better than inventing an agreement. No need to negotiate a final revenue split in this lesson.

questions.label: Which operating model are you exploring?
questions.hint: Describe who owns the car and who runs the rentals.
questions.example: Partnership idea: Jo owns the car and Maya runs the rental process.

questions.label: Who supplies and controls the vehicle?
questions.hint: Separate ownership from permission to schedule or release it.
questions.example: Jo supplies it; Maya’s booking authority is proposed, not yet agreed.

questions.label: Who handles bookings, maintenance and customer issues?
questions.hint: Give each job a role, even if one person does all three.
questions.example: Maya: bookings and messages. Jo: proposed service scheduling.

questions.label: Who pays expenses and covers downtime?
questions.hint: Identify who pays when the vehicle is unavailable, or mark the decision open.
questions.example: Repair costs and lost rental days are unresolved; both owners will review the arrangement.

questions.label: What permissions, coverage or written terms are still needed?
questions.hint: List the missing answer, responsible person and next action.
questions.example: Maya will confirm permitted rental use and coverage; both owners will seek review of responsibilities before agreeing.

lessons.done: Choose one model and assign the main jobs. An honest unresolved row is better than inventing an agreement. No need to negotiate a final revenue split in this lesson.
lessons.local: Check actual ownership, lender/lease permissions, coverage and the proposed agreement for your operating model.
lessons.time: Plan 10–15 minutes for a first draft; outside research can take longer.

lessons.title: Understand Your Costs
lessons.output: A simple cost list and a checked break-even calculation.
lessons.bring: A calculator. Use the supplied numbers before gathering your own quotes.
paragraphs: A rental rate is not your profit. First separate the costs that continue each month from costs that change with rentals.

Separate one-time setup spending, monthly fixed costs and costs that change with rentals. Write the amount, source/date and whether it is an estimate. Choose one unit: a paid rental day. Convert a per-trip expense before mixing units: a $30 cleaning cost spread over a three-day trip is $10 per paid day in that example. Keep this planning calculation separate from tax accounting.

Fictional math: $50 price − $20 variable cost = $30 contribution per paid day. Contribution is what remains toward fixed costs. $600 monthly fixed costs ÷ $30 = 20 paid days to cover those costs. At 15 paid days: 15 × $30 − $600 = −$150. If contribution is zero or negative, there is no positive break-even target using this formula. If the required paid days exceed available days, revise the plan.

Your task: List the three cost groups, then show the supplied calculation and the 15-day downside. Name excluded costs, such as startup recovery, owner time, financing and taxes; get help classifying your real costs without counting the same cost twice.

questions.label: What one-time setup costs might you have?
questions.hint: List amount, source/date and estimate or quote. Unknown amounts are acceptable.
questions.example: Cleaning supplies: $80, fictional estimate today. Vehicle preparation: unknown; request a quote.

questions.label: What costs continue each month?
questions.hint: List recurring bills and label estimates. Keep the car’s purchase price separate from monthly bills; get help classifying financing in your real plan.
questions.example: Practice operating model: $600/month fixed costs. Financing and accounting treatment excluded for later review.

questions.label: What costs change with rentals?
questions.hint: Use the same unit; show any per-trip to per-day conversion.
questions.example: Practice total: $20 per paid day. A $30 cleaning expense over three days would be $10/day within that total, not an extra $30/day.

questions.label: Calculate contribution and break-even days.
questions.hint: Use $600 fixed costs, $50/day price and $20/day variable cost.
questions.example: $50 − $20 = $30 per paid day. $600 ÷ $30 = 20 paid days.

questions.label: What happens at 15 paid days, and what is excluded?
questions.hint: Show the calculation and name costs this simplified model does not cover.
questions.example: 15 × $30 − $600 = −$150. Startup recovery, taxes, financing, owner time and surprises need separate review; refundable deposits are not earnings.

lessons.done: List the three cost groups, then show the supplied calculation and the 15-day downside. Name excluded costs, such as startup recovery, owner time, financing and taxes; get help classifying your real costs without counting the same cost twice.
lessons.local: Verify local taxes and charges separately. Ask an accountant how to classify financing, depreciation and owner compensation in your actual plan.

lessons.title: Build Your Business Plan
lessons.output: A one-page plan assembled from the work you already did.
lessons.bring: Your saved answers from 1.1–1.4; open “Earlier answers” in this lesson.
paragraphs: Your first business plan should help you decide what to do next. It does not need to be a long presentation.

Use four headings: customer and offer; vehicle and responsibilities; costs and resources; open decisions. Refer to your earlier worksheet answers instead of copying every line. Summarize only what matters for the next decision. For an open item, record a person, a next action and a review date. A planned launch date is not evidence that the open item is resolved.

Fictional plan: local repair customers; one compact car; Maya handles inquiries. Costs use the $600/$50/$20 practice model, not real quotes. Coverage and permitted use are unconfirmed. Next step: compare two vehicle candidates while Maya arranges coverage review. Research can continue; taking a paid booking is not the next step in this example.
Your task: Write five short summaries using your earlier work. End with one reversible next action. You do not need a pitch deck, a purchase or a finished legal setup.

questions.label: What do your customer and market notes say?
questions.hint: Refer to 1.1 and 1.2 and summarize the key finding in two lines.
questions.example: See 1.1: repair customers. See 1.2: fictional comparison only; real totals and demand still need research.

questions.label: What vehicle and operating model are proposed?
questions.hint: Bring forward 1.3 and name responsibilities still open.
questions.example: One compact car; Maya manages bookings. Vehicle ownership and expense responsibilities need review.

questions.label: What resources and costs matter first?
questions.hint: Use 1.4; identify assumptions instead of presenting them as quotes.
questions.example: The fictional model needs 20 paid days. Real insurance, vehicle and preparation costs are not yet quoted.

questions.label: Which open decisions need action?
questions.hint: Write one line per item: question → person → action → review date.
questions.example: Coverage → Maya → describe direct rentals to a licensed contact → review Friday.

questions.label: What is your next reversible step?
questions.hint: Choose research or preparation you can revise without committing to a purchase or rental.
questions.example: Compare two candidate cars and request missing cost information.

lessons.done: Write five short summaries using your earlier work. End with one reversible next action. You do not need a pitch deck, a purchase or a finished legal setup.
lessons.local: Carry your location, insurance and permission questions into the plan; a completed plan does not clear them.

lessons.title: Choose Vehicles for Your Market
lessons.output: A shortlist compared against the same three customer needs.
lessons.bring: Your target customer from 1.1 and cost assumptions from 1.4.
paragraphs: The best-looking vehicle is not automatically the best fit for your customer. Start with the job it needs to do.

Choose three must-have capabilities before browsing cars: for example, seating, luggage space and suitability for the intended trip. Compare two or three candidates against those same criteria. Keep a nice-to-have, such as a premium trim, separate. Record where specifications came from, then list maintenance, insurance and operating costs that still need research.

Fictional practice: Candidate A has the required seating and luggage space; its service history is missing. Candidate B meets the same requirements and has service records, but its operating cost is unknown. Both remain research candidates. You cannot declare B the better investment just because one document exists, or A unsuitable solely because its trim is basic.
Your task: Compare two candidates and choose which to investigate next. You are making a shortlist, not authorizing a purchase.

questions.label: Which customer need must the vehicle meet?
questions.hint: Use the situation from 1.1 rather than personal taste.
questions.example: Temporary local transport while the customer’s car is repaired.

questions.label: What are your three must-have capabilities?
questions.hint: Be concrete; separate essentials from attractive extras.
questions.example: Required seats, room for everyday bags and suitability for the intended local trips.

questions.label: Which two or three candidates will you compare?
questions.hint: Give each the same criteria and a specification source, or label practice data.
questions.example: Practice A and B both meet the three criteria. Real specifications still need manufacturer or vehicle-record confirmation.

questions.label: Which cost or maintenance facts are missing?
questions.hint: Name the missing information and where you would get it.
questions.example: A: service history missing. B: operating-cost estimate missing. Request records and quotes.

questions.label: Which candidate will you investigate next, and why?
questions.hint: A useful decision can be to hold both until one important fact is known.
questions.example: Investigate A’s history first; do not buy until the missing evidence is reviewed.

lessons.done: Compare two candidates and choose which to investigate next. You are making a shortlist, not authorizing a purchase.
lessons.time: Plan 10–15 minutes for a first draft; outside research can take longer.

lessons.title: Evaluate a Vehicle Before Committing
lessons.output: An evidence-based hold, reject or continue-evaluation decision.
lessons.bring: One candidate from 2.1. Use Training Car A for practice.
paragraphs: A vehicle can look clean and still have unresolved condition questions. Collect evidence before deciding.

Make three columns: seller statement, record or inspection evidence, and next action. Check vehicle identity, history, service records and recall information; arrange a qualified inspection. Keep source dates. NHTSA’s lookup is useful for recall research, but its result is not a full safety inspection or complete vehicle history. An unresolved concern needs a specific follow-up.

Practice record: Training Car A. Seller says “no work needed.” Service record is missing. A fictional inspector reports a concern requiring assessment; recall lookup has not been done. Decision: hold. Next actions: obtain missing records, check recall information and arrange the recommended assessment. Do not turn “not checked” into “passed.”
Your task: Separate the claim, evidence and missing checks for one car. Name the next action behind your decision. You do not have to buy or inspect a real car to finish this practice.

questions.label: Which vehicle are you evaluating?
questions.hint: Use a fictional name or private reference; do not put customer documents here.
questions.example: Training Car A from my candidate shortlist.

questions.label: What does the seller claim, and what supports it?
questions.hint: Pair each statement with a record, or write “unsupported.”
questions.example: Seller says no work needed. Service record missing, so that claim is unsupported.

questions.label: What history, service and recall checks are recorded?
questions.hint: List dates and sources. “Not checked; next action…” is valid.
questions.example: History: not checked. Service record: requested. Recall lookup: not done; owner to check the actual vehicle identifier privately.

questions.label: What does the inspection show?
questions.hint: Use the supplied practice finding if you do not have an inspection.
questions.example: Fictional inspector flagged a concern needing assessment; no clearance yet.

questions.label: Will you hold, reject or continue evaluating?
questions.hint: Give the evidence and next action; “continue evaluating” is not “ready to rent.”
questions.example: Hold. Obtain the records and qualified assessment before reconsidering.

lessons.done: Separate the claim, evidence and missing checks for one car. Name the next action behind your decision. You do not have to buy or inspect a real car to finish this practice.
lessons.local: Verify vehicle use, registration and inspection requirements for your location. Recall lookup alone does not establish readiness.

lessons.title: Evaluate Purchase, Financing, Lease, or Partnership Options
lessons.output: A side-by-side comparison of two ways to obtain a vehicle.
lessons.bring: Two real quotes or clearly labeled fictional options.
paragraphs: A smaller monthly payment can hide a different total commitment. Compare the whole arrangement before choosing.

Compare upfront cash, number and amount of payments, ownership at the end, permitted rental use, maintenance duties and exit costs. A low monthly payment can accompany a long or restricted commitment. Keep financing/lease terms and estimates separate. Ask the provider to clarify the actual contract; personal-use terms do not establish rental-use permission.

Fictional cash-outlay exercise: A costs $12,000 upfront. B costs $2,000 upfront plus 24 payments of $450: $12,800 scheduled cash outlay. This does not make A automatically better: fees, ownership at the end, maintenance, risk and permitted use are not specified. Both need review. The numbers are arithmetic practice, not an available finance offer.
Your task: Use the same comparison fields for two options. Identify the missing facts that prevent a decision, especially rental-use permission and exit obligations.

questions.label: Which two acquisition options are you comparing?
questions.hint: Name the type and whether the data is real or fictional.
questions.example: Fictional A: upfront purchase. Fictional B: payment arrangement with ownership terms unknown.

questions.label: What cash and payment commitments does each require?
questions.hint: Include upfront amount, payment count and term; do not compare only monthly payments.
questions.example: A: $12,000 upfront. B: $2,000 + 24 × $450 = $12,800 scheduled cash outlay before unspecified costs.

questions.label: Who pays maintenance, insurance and downtime?
questions.hint: For each option, record the proposed responsibility or “unknown.”
questions.example: A and B: costs and responsibilities need written confirmation.

questions.label: What rental-use and exit conditions need checking?
questions.hint: Include ownership at the end, early exit and any restrictions.
questions.example: B: rental permission, ownership transfer and early-exit terms are unknown. A: permitted rental use still needs checks.

questions.label: What evidence do you need before deciding?
questions.hint: Name the document or reviewer and one next action.
questions.example: Obtain complete written terms for both; review use permission and total commitments before choosing.

lessons.done: Use the same comparison fields for two options. Identify the missing facts that prevent a decision, especially rental-use permission and exit obligations.
lessons.local: Use the actual lender, lessor or partner’s written terms and qualified review; this exercise does not recommend a finance product.

lessons.title: Prepare a Vehicle for Rental
lessons.output: A vehicle preparation checklist with a clear hold or ready-for-review status.
lessons.bring: Your evaluation from 2.2; one practice vehicle.
paragraphs: Preparing a vehicle means more than washing it and taking listing photos. Build a record someone else could follow.

Work in four groups: documents and service; cleaning; equipment and keys; baseline condition. Give each item a status, responsible person and evidence reference. “Available” means the calendar is open; it does not mean the car is ready. A warning indicator or unresolved service issue belongs in the hold list until qualified assessment resolves it.

Practice record: Training Car A is cleaned, keys counted and overview photos taken. A warning indicator remains unresolved. Maya is responsible for arranging assessment. The status remains on hold. The listing photos are complete, but they do not clear the warning or replace a current pickup condition record.
Your task: Create one checklist and name the issue that prevents release. Record what evidence would let the responsible reviewer reconsider it.

questions.label: Which vehicle are you preparing?
questions.hint: Keep the same private or fictional reference as your evaluation.
questions.example: Training Car A; see my 2.2 evaluation.

questions.label: What documents and service checks are ready or open?
questions.hint: Use item → status → evidence → person.
questions.example: Service concern → open → assessment pending → Maya. Vehicle-use documents → not verified → owner to review.

questions.label: What cleaning, equipment and key checks are assigned?
questions.hint: A short checklist with names or roles is enough.
questions.example: Maya checks interior, exterior, agreed equipment and key count; records date and result.

questions.label: Where will the baseline condition record go?
questions.hint: Name a private record location; listing photos and pickup records have different purposes.
questions.example: Private vehicle folder, linked to Training Car A; current pickup photos will be stored with each rental.

questions.label: What keeps this vehicle on hold?
questions.hint: Name the concern and the evidence needed to reconsider it.
questions.example: Warning indicator unresolved. Qualified assessment and documented resolution are needed before a readiness review.

lessons.done: Create one checklist and name the issue that prevents release. Record what evidence would let the responsible reviewer reconsider it.
lessons.local: Check applicable vehicle documents, operating permissions, coverage and inspection requirements before release.

lessons.title: Organize Your Business Setup
lessons.output: A setup research list with a source and next action for each question.
lessons.bring: Your operating locations from 0.2 and model from 1.3.
paragraphs: A business name is one part of setup. Build a location-specific checklist instead of assuming registration finishes the job.

Create rows for business identity, operating permissions, taxes and recordkeeping. Start with official state business-registration, state revenue, local city/county and vehicle-agency resources relevant to your activity. For a special pickup site, identify who controls it. These are research starting points, not a complete list of requirements. Use status labels: not checked, submitted, pending or confirmed with evidence.

Fictional example: Maya has submitted a business-name application but has not received confirmation. She also plans pickup at a location whose permission is unknown. These are two separate rows. The application receipt supports “submitted,” not “approved.” Maya records the relevant office, question, contact date and the evidence she needs. Tax/entity choices go to the appropriate adviser.
Your task: Write a short research list, using your actual planned locations. Your goal today is to know who to ask and what evidence to keep, not complete every registration.

questions.label: Where and how do you intend to operate?
questions.hint: Bring forward the location and model notes; include proposed delivery areas.
questions.example: Local direct rentals in my recorded city/county/state; airport delivery not yet offered.

questions.label: Which setup questions need answers?
questions.hint: Start with identity, permissions, tax registration and recordkeeping; this is not an exhaustive compliance checklist.
questions.example: Business registration status, pickup-location permission and applicable rental tax questions.

questions.label: Which official source or contact will you use for each?
questions.hint: Name the office and exact question; save a source link/date privately.
questions.example: State business office: registration. City/county office: pickup site. State revenue office: rental tax questions.

questions.label: Which business details must match across records?
questions.hint: List fields, not sensitive identification numbers.
questions.example: Legal business name, public trading name where applicable, business contact and approved address details.

questions.label: What proves each item’s status?
questions.hint: Distinguish an application receipt from an issued approval.
questions.example: Registration: submitted, receipt retained. Pickup permission: not checked, owner to contact the office Friday.

lessons.done: Write a short research list, using your actual planned locations. Your goal today is to know who to ask and what evidence to keep, not complete every registration.

lessons.title: Create a Trustworthy Brand and Listing
lessons.output: A factual listing draft with one clear next step.
lessons.bring: Your customer, candidate vehicle and proposed pickup process.
paragraphs: Your listing should help a customer decide whether the rental fits. Attractive photos cannot fix unclear terms.

Build five parts: headline, vehicle facts, what is included, pickup process and how to request dates. Use accurate current photos and supported specifications. Separate offered services from ideas under review. Make important price conditions visible rather than hiding them behind a vague “from” number. Do not publish a practice listing or invent reviews to fill gaps.

Fictional draft: “Compact car for temporary local transport. Request your dates for an itemized quote. Local pickup by confirmed appointment. Included items and mileage are shown in the quote. Delivery is not currently offered.” Before using it, Maya must confirm the actual vehicle facts, pickup permission, pricing disclosures and ability to provide the service. A friend can read the draft and explain what to do next.
Your task: Write the short draft, list supporting photos/facts and identify claims to verify. Keep it unpublished until those checks are complete.

questions.label: What is your factual headline and description?
questions.hint: Say what the car/service is; avoid unsupported “best,” “fully covered” or guaranteed availability claims.
questions.example: Practice: Compact car for temporary local transport. Request dates for a quote.

questions.label: Which photos and specifications support the description?
questions.hint: List current images and sources; do not use an unrelated vehicle as the actual listing.
questions.example: Current exterior/interior photos and verified seating/cargo details from the actual vehicle record.

questions.label: What is included, optional or unavailable?
questions.hint: Use separate short lines so conditions are visible.
questions.example: Included items: to verify in quote. Delivery: not currently offered. Mileage: stated in reviewed terms.

questions.label: How does pickup work, and what should a customer do next?
questions.hint: One clear action is enough.
questions.example: Local pickup by confirmed appointment; request pickup and return dates first.

questions.label: What must be verified before publishing?
questions.hint: Read each factual claim back against its evidence.
questions.example: Vehicle details, actual availability, pickup permission, price disclosures and included items.

lessons.title: Set and Review Your Pricing
lessons.output: An itemized practice quote with unknown items visible.
lessons.bring: Your cost exercise from 1.4 and comparison notes from 1.2.
paragraphs: Copying a competitor’s price tells you nothing about whether it works for your costs. Build a quote you can explain.

Start with daily rate × agreed daily units. Show selected options separately. Then identify any taxes, allowed charges and refundable amounts that need verification. A deposit and rental charge are different lines. Do not call an incomplete subtotal a final total. This exercise uses fixed three-day units; your real pricing must explain how pickup/return times affect billing.

Fictional quote: three days × $50 = $150 base. Optional delivery, if selected in this separate example: $30. Subtotal with that option: $180 before any applicable verified taxes or other charges. Deposit terms are unknown and shown separately. Neither $150 nor $180 is an all-inclusive final quote. In the later R-001 practice rental, delivery is not selected.

questions.label: What supports your proposed base rate?
questions.hint: Bring together cost and market notes; label practice numbers and gaps.
questions.example: The $50/day rate is fictional for arithmetic. Actual cost quotes and comparable rental totals still need research.

questions.hint: Show the multiplication so another person can check it.

questions.label: What is the subtotal with a $30 delivery option?
questions.hint: Add the option only when selected; this is a hypothetical option.
questions.example: $150 + $30 = $180 before applicable verified taxes or other charges.

questions.label: Which taxes, fees or deposit terms need checking?
questions.hint: Keep unknowns visible; do not invent a final payable amount.
questions.example: Taxes and allowed charges unknown; deposit amount and handling unverified. No all-inclusive total yet.

questions.label: How would fewer paid days affect the monthly plan?
questions.hint: Reuse the $600/$50/$20 example; do not count deposits as earnings.

A relevant inquiry matches the service and dates you could potentially offer; it is not proof of eligibility or a booking. Test an idea without claiming a partnership or outcome that does not exist.

Fictional test: Maya spends one hour this week on two research conversations with repair shops, with no paid ad spend. She records recurring customer questions. If both conversations mention difficulty understanding total price, she revises her listing draft and plans a further test. questions.hint: Choose one audience and one channel, not every social platform.

questions.hint: Match the next action to the test: a question for research or an inquiry for a reviewed offer.

questions.label: What is the time or spending limit?
questions.hint: Set a boundary you can afford; do not assume paid advertising is required.

questions.label: How will you separate interest from bookings?
questions.hint: Record source and stage; a view or inquiry is not a confirmed rental.

questions.label: What would make you continue, revise or stop?
questions.hint: Name a measurable signal and a review date.
questions.example: Review Friday: use repeated questions to revise the offer; do not scale from two conversations alone.

lessons.title: Turn Inquiries into Bookings
lessons.output: A short inquiry response and a recorded follow-up.
lessons.bring: A fictional customer question; your quote and process notes.
paragraphs: An inquiry is a conversation, not a confirmed rental. Help the customer understand the steps without promising an unchecked booking.

Use a four-part reply: acknowledge the request, ask for missing dates/times and pickup needs, explain the next step, and state what is still pending. Check the schedule and vehicle readiness before confirming availability. Share the reviewed quote and requirements before asking the customer to commit. Collect sensitive information only through your appropriate secure process.

Practice inquiry: “Do you have a car this weekend?” Reply: “What pickup and return dates/times do you need, and will you collect locally? I’ll check the vehicle schedule and send the quote and rental requirements. Your booking is not confirmed yet.” Record the next action: staff checks the schedule after the dates arrive. Do not request card or identity-document details in the course worksheet.
Your task: Write a concise reply and a follow-up status. The customer should understand both their next step and what you will check.

questions.label: What did the fictional customer ask?
questions.hint: Keep the original question visible.
questions.example: Do you have a car this weekend?

questions.label: What details are missing?
questions.hint: Ask only what is needed to clarify the request now.
questions.example: Exact pickup/return dates and times, vehicle needs and pickup location.

questions.label: What must you check before confirming?
questions.hint: Include schedule, vehicle readiness and the reviewed quote/requirements.
questions.example: Calendar conflicts, readiness, pickup arrangements and the correct itemized quote.

questions.label: What is your short response?
questions.hint: Give one clear next action without claiming a booking exists.
questions.example: Please send your dates/times and pickup needs. I’ll check availability and send the quote and requirements; the booking is not confirmed yet.

questions.label: What follow-up will you record?
questions.hint: Use status → person → next action.
questions.example: Inquiry awaiting dates → staff → check schedule when details arrive.

lessons.done: Write a concise reply and a follow-up status. The customer should understand both their next step and what you will check.

lessons.title: Complete Pickup and Vehicle Handoff
lessons.output: A pickup record and an explicit release-or-hold decision.
lessons.bring: R-001. First review the unresolved checks from 5.1–5.3.
paragraphs: Before you hand over the keys, take pickup photos and review them with your renter.

First decide whether the required release checks are resolved. If not, record hold. To practice the physical handoff, this fictional scenario then explicitly supplies: corrected reservation and agreement, verified signing/payment evidence, qualified resolution of the vehicle concern and the required release review. These are training assumptions only, not facts about your business. Record them before rehearsing the pickup.

Pickup practice: R-001, Day 1 at 09:00; Training Car A shows 42,800 miles and a full fuel indication. A left-front wheel mark already exists. Record overview images plus a detail and wider location image of the mark; link them to R-001 and this pickup time. Review the mark and condition record with Alex. paragraphs: When a renter asks for a change, record the request before changing the rental. A conversation is not the whole decision.

Record what changed, when it was requested and what the renter wants. For an extension, check schedule conflicts, approved terms, coverage and any signing/payment changes. An extension request is not approval. Until a change is properly confirmed, keep the original arrangement visible. If it needs review, tell the renter who is checking it and when you plan to update them.

Message: “We cannot extend this vehicle because it is booked next. Your agreed return remains Day 4 at 09:00. Contact us if you need to discuss the return arrangements.” Do not quietly move the next customer’s booking.

Observations, proposed charges and completed financial actions are separate. Review any adjustment against original evidence, the agreement and applicable rules. Use actual provider statuses for deposit/refund handling; do not promise when money reaches a bank.

Practice return: Day 4 at 09:00; 42,950 miles; full fuel indication. The same left-front wheel mark appears in pickup and return images; no new mark is established by these records. This exercise leaves financial closeout pending those checks.

lessons.title: Handle Cancellations, No-Shows, and Late Returns
lessons.output: A calm response to one cancellation, no-show or late-return scenario.
lessons.bring: A policy process from 3.5; use the separate exception example below.
paragraphs: When plans change, use the recorded facts and your reviewed policy. Do not improvise a penalty in the middle of a disagreement.

Name the event first: cancellation, no-show, late pickup or late return. Create a short timeline of agreed times, messages and actual events. Check the policy version and applicable requirements before deciding any adjustment. Keep a request, approval and completed payment action separate. This exercise uses a different branch from R-001’s on-time return.

Fictional late-return branch: return agreed at 09:00; renter requested extra time at 08:30; no approval was given; at 09:30 the car has not returned. Staff records the facts and contacts the renter through the reviewed procedure. Message: “Our record shows return was due at 09:00 and no extension is confirmed. Please update us on your return status.” The owner reviews the situation; no invented grace period, fee or recovery tactic is added.
Your task: Write the timeline, decision-maker and message for one exception. Leave unverified charges or escalation requirements open for the appropriate reviewer.

questions.label: Which exception occurred, and when?
questions.hint: Distinguish this alternate practice branch from the normal R-001 closeout.
questions.example: Separate late-return scenario: due 09:00; request 08:30; no approval; still absent 09:30.

questions.label: Which terms and messages support the timeline?
questions.hint: Use original records; do not convert a request into permission.

questions.label: Which policy and location checks are needed?
questions.hint: Identify the applicable version and unresolved requirements.
questions.example: Reviewed late-return policy version needed; applicable notice/adjustment requirements still to verify.

questions.label: Who decides the next action?
questions.hint: Separate staff contact from authority to approve adjustments or escalation.
questions.example: Staff contacts renter; owner reviews the facts and any allowed next steps with appropriate help.

questions.label: What calm message will you send?
questions.hint: Ask for relevant information; avoid threats or unsupported fees.
questions.example: Our record shows return due at 09:00 with no confirmed extension. Please update us on your return status.

lessons.title: Respond to Breakdowns, Accidents, and Damage Reports
lessons.output: An incident contact plan and a first-response message.
lessons.bring: Use fictional contact placeholders; keep real emergency/insurer details privately.
paragraphs: An incident response should begin with immediate safety and appropriate help, not an argument about who will pay.

Prepare contacts before a trip: local emergency services, approved roadside assistance, insurer reporting and the responsible business person. In an actual emergency, contact local emergency services and follow their instructions. Ask what help is needed, gather facts only when safe, and follow the verified assistance/reporting process. Staff should not diagnose a car by text or decide fault or coverage.

Practice report: “A warning appeared and the car is stopped.” Response: “Is anyone in immediate danger or needing emergency help? If so, contact local emergency services. When safe, use our verified assistance contact; we will coordinate the next update.” Record the reported condition, assistance reference and responsible person. Do not tell the renter to continue driving a potentially unsafe vehicle or promise the insurer will pay.
Your task: List the contact roles, facts to record and next-update owner. Identify any real instructions you still need to confirm before using this plan.

questions.label: Which verified contacts will you keep privately?
questions.hint: Use roles here, not real phone numbers or incident locations.
questions.example: Local emergency services; approved roadside provider; insurer reporting contact; on-duty business contact.

questions.label: Which response instructions still need confirmation?
questions.hint: Use the actual provider/insurer process; do not invent a roadside procedure.
questions.example: Confirm emergency escalation, approved towing/assistance, insurer reporting steps and after-hours responsibility.

questions.label: What can you record when safe?
questions.hint: Stick to what was reported and observed; do not assign fault or diagnose.
questions.example: Report time, reported warning/stopped vehicle, whether help is requested and assistance reference. Location kept privately.

questions.label: Who handles reporting and the vehicle’s return to service?
questions.hint: Separate insurer reporting from qualified vehicle assessment.
questions.example: Designated owner handles reporting; qualified service reviewer assesses vehicle readiness before it is offered again.

questions.label: What acknowledgment and update plan will you use?
questions.hint: Put immediate help first, then state who will follow up.
questions.example: Is immediate emergency help needed? When safe, follow the verified assistance route. The on-duty contact will coordinate and tell you the next update time.

lessons.title: Resolve Payment Issues and Customer Complaints
lessons.output: An evidence-based complaint response with an owner and next action.
lessons.bring: Use the separate fuel-charge complaint below.
paragraphs: A complaint is easier to review when the facts are organized. Start by understanding the disputed item, not defending every decision.

Identify exactly what the customer disputes: amount, service or event. Gather original quote/agreement, messages, condition evidence and payment history. Note gaps rather than filling them with assumptions. If a formal payment dispute exists, check the provider portal and its actual response deadline; a customer email alone does not satisfy that process. Keep complaint resolution and provider actions recorded separately.

Fictional case: a renter questions a fuel charge. Pickup shows full, but the return fuel photo is missing. That is an evidence gap, not permission to invent a reading. Staff asks the authorized reviewer to examine the charge and any correction. Message: “I’m reviewing the fuel charge against the original records. The return evidence is incomplete; I’ll update you after the review.” Do not condition routine resolution on deleting a review.
Your task: Name the disputed item, evidence gap, reviewer and next message. If there is a formal dispute, record its real deadline privately rather than guessing one.

questions.label: What exactly is disputed?
questions.hint: Use a separate fictional case; do not change R-001’s recorded full-fuel return.
questions.example: Separate practice case: renter disputes a fuel charge.

questions.label: Which original records exist, and what is missing?
questions.hint: Separate the policy from evidence of the actual event.
questions.example: Pickup fuel photo exists; return fuel photo missing. Agreement and messages need review.

questions.label: Which instructions or deadlines need checking?
questions.hint: Distinguish a complaint from a formal provider dispute.
questions.example: Check whether a formal dispute exists; if it does, use the provider’s actual submission process/deadline.

questions.label: Who can approve a correction or response?
questions.hint: Identify authority; staff should not invent evidence to defend a charge.
questions.example: Authorized owner reviews the unsupported item and decides the documented response or correction.

questions.label: What will you tell the customer, and what happens next?
questions.hint: Acknowledge the specific issue and avoid claiming an uncompleted refund.
questions.example: I’m reviewing the fuel charge; return evidence is incomplete. The owner will check the records and provide the outcome. No refund is confirmed yet.

lessons.title: Review Your Business Performance
lessons.output: A one-period review with two clearly defined utilization numbers.
lessons.bring: A calculator and the supplied fictional 30-day month.
paragraphs: A busy calendar can hide weak results. Review the numbers using definitions you can apply consistently.

Utilization describes how much of a chosen time period was rented; always name the denominator, the number you divide by. For this exercise, available-day utilization = paid rental days ÷ available days. Calendar-day utilization = paid rental days ÷ all calendar days. Track downtime separately, then compare revenue with costs. These percentages alone do not establish profit.

Practice month: 30 calendar days, 10 unavailable days and 15 paid days. Available days = 30 − 10 = 20. Available-day utilization = 15 ÷ 20 = 75%. Calendar-day utilization = 15 ÷ 30 = 50%. Five available days were unpaid. If no days are available, the first ratio is undefined, not zero or 100%. Investigate the ten unavailable days before buying another car.
Your task: Calculate both percentages, separate revenue/deposits/expenses and choose one improvement to investigate next period. Use the same definitions for comparisons.

questions.label: What period and definitions will you use?
questions.hint: State the dates/length and what counts as paid, available and unavailable.
questions.example: Fictional 30-day month. Paid: 15 rented days. Unavailable: 10 days out of service. Available: 20 days including paid days.

questions.label: Calculate both utilization percentages.
questions.hint: Show the denominator in each calculation.
questions.example: Available-day: 15 ÷ (30 − 10) = 75%. Calendar-day: 15 ÷ 30 = 50%. Five available days were unpaid.

questions.label: Which money records stay separate?
questions.hint: Keep refundable funds and expense records distinct from rental revenue.
questions.example: Rental charges, collected taxes, refundable funds, refunds and business expenses tracked separately; cash balance is not profit.

questions.label: What downtime or customer issue needs investigation?
questions.hint: Link the question to a record rather than assuming the cause.
questions.example: Why was the car unavailable for ten days? Review service and scheduling records.

questions.label: What one improvement will you test?
questions.hint: Name one change and a later comparison; do not promise higher earnings.
questions.example: Review service scheduling to reduce avoidable delays, then compare unavailable days next period.

lessons.done: Calculate both percentages, separate revenue/deposits/expenses and choose one improvement to investigate next period. Use the same definitions for comparisons.

Use the actual manufacturer information, vehicle history and qualified service advice to determine due work. List item, responsible person, service date and expected unavailable time. Block that time in the real scheduling process and review affected bookings. Service completed and vehicle cleared for return are related checks; retain the record supporting the readiness decision.

Fictional example: Training Car A has a recurring concern, and assessment is scheduled on Day 8. Maya marks it unavailable while the concern is assessed and checks upcoming reservations. Return-to-service evidence is still needed; a completed calendar appointment alone does not clear it. questions.hint: A completed appointment alone is not clearance.

questions.label: What records help decide eventual replacement?
questions.hint: Gather a pattern over time rather than deciding from one repair.
questions.example: Repair history, total costs, unavailable days and fit for the customer’s needs.

lessons.title: Build Your Team and Daily Procedures
lessons.output: A one-task procedure another person can follow.
lessons.bring: Choose pickup, return inspection or reservation review.
paragraphs: Giving someone a login is not the same as giving them a clear job. Define the task, decision limit and handoff.

Write the task as a short sequence, then name who performs it, who reviews exceptions and what record shows it is complete. Specify necessary access and escalation. Use separate accounts where supported, and verify actual permissions before relying on them. A proposed role in a worksheet does not configure software access. Keep employment/contractor decisions separate for qualified review.

Practice procedure: staff identifies R-001, records return time/condition/readings, attaches evidence and flags any mismatch. The owner reviews proposed charges. Staff does not need billing-administration access simply to record condition. Rehearse with fictional data, then change the steps that caused confusion. When a role changes, reassign open work and remove access no longer needed.

questions.hint: Choose one task with a clear start and finish.

questions.hint: Give roles rather than relying on “someone handles it.”
